Minimum Risk Point Estimation of the Population Standardized Mean Difference

Source: R/mr_smd.R
mr_smd.Rd

A function for the sequential estimation of the standardized mean difference with minimum risk. The function implements the procedure of Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2017), which considers study cost and the accuracy of the estimated standardized mean difference together. mr_smd assumes normally distributed data, equal sample sizes in the two groups, and an equal cost of sampling per observation in each group.

Usage

mr_smd(
  A,
  structural_cost,
  epsilon,
  d,
  n_per_group,
  sampling_cost,
  pilot = FALSE,
  m0 = 4,
  gamma = 0.49
)

Arguments

A

The structural cost divided by the square of epsilon: the price one is willing to pay for a maximum allowable difference of epsilon between the estimate of the standardized mean difference and its parameter, a single positive number. Give either A or both structural_cost and epsilon.

structural_cost

The structural cost of what one is willing to pay in a study, a single positive number.

epsilon

The maximum desired difference between the estimated standardized mean difference and the population value, a single positive number.

d

The current estimate of the standardized mean difference, a single finite number. It is needed when pilot = FALSE.

n_per_group

Current sample size per group (thus total sample size is \(2n\)), a whole number of at least 2; requires equal sample size per group. It is needed when pilot = FALSE.

sampling_cost

The cost of collecting one more observation, a single positive number. For example, if each survey costs 10 dollars to distribute and score, sampling_cost would be 10 dollars per additional observation.

pilot

TRUE to plan the pilot sample size per group, or FALSE (the default) to evaluate the risk function and the stopping rule at the current sample size.

m0

The smallest pilot sample size per group allowed: a whole number of at least 4 (the default).

gamma

The exponent \(\gamma\) of the correction term \(n^{-\gamma}\) in the stopping rule, which keeps sampling from stopping too early: a single number strictly between 0 and 1/2. Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2017) take \(0 < \gamma < 1/2\) and suggest .49 for practical purposes, the default.

Value

A dmar_tbl with columns term and value. With pilot = FALSE the rows are

risk

The estimated risk at the current sample size, \(A V_n^2 / n + 2cn\).

n_1

Sample size for group 1 (the input n_per_group).

n_2

Sample size for group 2 (the input n_per_group).

d

The input estimate of the standardized mean difference.

The attribute is_satisfied is TRUE when the stopping rule is satisfied, so that sampling can stop, and the attribute criterion holds \(\sqrt{A / (2c)}\,(V_n + n^{-\gamma})\), the value that the sample size per group is compared with. The decision is printed under the table: whether the stopping rule is met, the two numbers compared, and whether to stop or to collect another observation in each group. With pilot = TRUE the single row is pilot_n_per_group (see Note).

Details

Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2017) estimate the population standardized mean difference sequentially, minimizing a risk function that adds the mean square error of the estimator, weighted by A, to the total sampling cost. With \(n\) observations per group and \(V_n^2 = 2 + d^2/4\), sampling stops at the first \(n\) for which \(n \ge \sqrt{A / (2c)}\,(V_n + n^{-\gamma})\), where \(c\) is sampling_cost. With pilot = FALSE the function evaluates that risk and the stopping rule at the current sample size; with pilot = TRUE it returns the pilot sample size per group, \(\max(m_0, \lceil (A / (2c))^{1/(2 + 2\gamma)} \rceil)\). A formula value that is itself a whole number is that number, although R can compute it a little above (with \(A = 1{,}000{,}000\), \(c = 5\), and \(\gamma = .25\) it is 100, not 101; see mr_cv). See Kelley and Rausch (2006) for additional information on the standardized mean difference.

Note

When pilot=TRUE the function returns one row, pilot_n_per_group: the size of the pilot sample per group that should be used (thus, the total sample size is twice the pilot sample size).

References

Chattopadhyay, B., & Kelley, K. (2016). Estimation of the coefficient of variation with minimum risk: A sequential method for minimizing sampling error and study cost. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 51(5), 627–648. doi:10.1080/00273171.2016.1203279

Chattopadhyay, B., & Kelley, K. (2017). Estimating the standardized mean difference with minimum risk: Maximizing accuracy and minimizing cost with sequential estimation. Psychological Methods, 22(1), 94–113. doi:10.1037/met0000089

Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2018). Accuracy in parameter estimation for a general class of effect sizes: A sequential approach. Psychological Methods, 23(2), 226–243. doi:10.1037/met0000127

Kelley, K., & Rausch, J. R. (2006). Sample size planning for the standardized mean difference: Accuracy in parameter estimation via narrow confidence intervals. Psychological Methods, 11(4), 363–385. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.11.4.363

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge.

See also

ci_smd, mr_cv

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# To obtain pilot sample size in a situation in which A=10000. Note that 'A' is
# 'structural_cost' divided by the square of 'epsilon'.

# From Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2017)
mr_smd(pilot = TRUE, A = 10000, sampling_cost = 2.4, gamma = .49)
#>  term              value
#>  pilot_n_per_group 13   

High.SLS <- c(11, 7, 22, 13, 6, 9, 11, 16, 12, 17, 14, 8, 16)
Low.SLS <- c(3, 6, 10, 8, 14, 5, 12, 10, 6, 8, 13, 5, 9)

mr_smd(d = 1.021484, n_per_group = 13, A = 10000, sampling_cost = 2.40, gamma = .49)
#>  term value   
#>  risk 1801.521
#>  n_1  13      
#>  n_2  13      
#>  d    1.021   
#> 
#> Stopping rule: not met (the sample size per group, 13, is below the criterion, 81.618); collect another observation in each group.

# Or, using the smd() function:
mr_smd(d = smd(group_1 = High.SLS, group_2 = Low.SLS)[1,2], n_per_group = 13, A = 10000,
       sampling_cost = 2.40, gamma = .49)
#>  term value   
#>  risk 1801.521
#>  n_1  13      
#>  n_2  13      
#>  d    1.021   
#> 
#> Stopping rule: not met (the sample size per group, 13, is below the criterion, 81.618); collect another observation in each group.

# Here, for this situation, the stopping rule is satisfied:
mr_smd(d = 1.00, n_per_group = 75, A = 10000, sampling_cost = 2.40, gamma = .49)
#>  term value
#>  risk 660  
#>  n_1  75   
#>  n_2  75   
#>  d    1    
#> 
#> Stopping rule: met (the sample size per group, 75, is at least the criterion, 73.968); sampling can stop.
